Final Summary Decision;
JRS Motion for Summary Judgement Denied
Counsel of record for Appellant, JRS Properties III LLLP dba Cedar Creek Cattle
(“JRS”) timely filed its Motion For Summary Judgment (“JRS Motion”) on May 17, 2021,
pursuant to the schedule therefor set out in my Scheduling Order dated March 17, 2021.
In turn, pursuant to that same order, JRS timely filed its Response Brief (“JRS
Response”) on June 17, 2021, and subsequently timely filed its Reply Brief (“JRS Reply”)
on July 1, 2021. JRS’s Motion covers: (1) the Bureau of Land Management’s (“BLM”)
10

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
Revised Environmental Assessment (“EA”), including its associated Finding Of No
Significant Impact (“FONSI”), both of which are dated February 28, 2020, and (2) BLM’s
two Final Decisions dated June 15, 2020, which implicate the following six dockets: ID-
JFO-2020-043, ID-JFO-2020-045, ID-JFO-2020-046, ID-JFO-2020-048, ID-JFO-2020-064,
and ID-JFO-2020-066, which variously cover the Coonskin -EJD Allotment and the
Pigtail Butte Allotment.
As stated in the JRS Motion, “This Motion is specific to a single issue, commonly
referred to as the ‘Record Issue’, previously commented upon by the Hearings Division
in the ALJ Order dated March 17, 2021, at pages 11-12, and in the ALJ Order dated May
3, 2021, at pages 13-15. See also: Order dated April 9, 2021, ALJ Order dated April 19,
2021. The ALJ Orders assist in bracketing the ‘Record Issue’ addressed in this Motion.”
JRS Motion, p. 4. The JRS Motion also attaches the Declaration of Darcy A. Helmick
(“Helmick Declaration”), dated May 17, 2021, as Attachment #1.
BLM’s Motion for Summary Judgment (“BLM’s Motion”) regarding JRS was
also timely filed on May 17, 2021, pursuant to the schedule set out in my Scheduling
Order dated March 17, 2021. In turn, pursuant to that same order, BLM timely filed its
Response Brief (“BLM Response”) on June 17, 2021, and also subsequently timely filed
its Reply Brief (“BLM Reply”) on July 1, 2021. WWP and Wildlands Defense timely
filed their Motions For Summary Judgment, with attached briefs, on May 17, 2021. In
turn, they timely filed their Response Briefs on June 17, 2021. WWP timely filed its
Reply Brief early on June 25, 2021. And, Wildlands Defense timely filed its Reply Brief
on July 1, 2021. Consequently, the JRS Motion For Summary Judgment is now ripe for
Summary Decision.
BACKGROUND
The Pigtail Butte Allotment is in the southeast portion of the Devil Creek
Subregion and includes 30,581 acres divided into eleven pastures. Guerry Final
Decision, p. 4, BER 043701. BLM administered public lands are 28,462 acres, Idaho state
lands are 1,280 acres, and there are 839 acres of private land. Revised EA, p. 6. Under
the expiring permits, the average yearly actual use in the Pigtail Butte Allotment was
2,580 AUMs, which included 1,344 AUMs on the part of JRS and 1,236 AUMs by
Guerry, Inc., with an average of 1,676 cattle grazed between March 1 and February 28
by JRS and Guerry. JRS Final Decision (June 15, 2020), p. 6.
The Coonskin-AMD Allotment is in the north central portion of the Devil Creek
Subregion and is composed of 42,809 acres divided into seven pastures. BLM public
lands are 41,054 acres, Idaho state lands are 1,281 acres, and there are 474 acres of
11

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
privately owned land. Revised EA, pp. 126-127. The East Juniper Draw Allotment
abuts the Coonskin Allotment to the east and is composed of 24,051 acres divided into
six pastures. BLM public lands are 20,705 acres, Idaho state lands are 1,280 acres, and
there are 2,065 acres of privately owned land. Ibid. Under the Guerry Final Decision on
appeal, Guerry is authorized to graze up to 3,255 AUMs, representing 7,821 sheep or
1,564 cattle, between March 1 and February 28 each year on pastures that composed the
former Coonskin Allotment. Guerry Final Decision, pp. 10-11. Relatedly, under the JRS
Final Decision on appeal, JRS is authorized to graze up to 2,182 cattle, 10,259 AUMs,
across the entire newly combined Coonskin-EJD Allotment from March 1 to February
28. JRS Final Decision, p. 7.
BLM also authorized the installation of range improvements to facilitate grazing.
Included are some 3.1 miles of new pipeline and three new trough sites in three
separate pastures. And, all fences within 1.2 miles of occupied lek sites must be marked
with collision diverter devices. Guerry Final Decision, pp. 18-19; JRS Final Decision, pp.
18-19.
By way of further background, BLM began the permit renewal process for the
subject allotments in the Devil Creek Subregion by reviewing the Pigtail Butte
Rangeland Health Assessment, pp. 59-136; BER 177386-177463. As pointed out in
BLM’s Motion , “The data showed that within the subregion, wildfire was the major
influencer on rangeland health. Wildfire led to significant reductions in shrub-
dominated vegetation communities … .” BLM Motion, p. 2. During the following two
years, BLM invited applications from the permittees on the subject allotments. BLM
prepared it’s Proposed EA, which analyzed the impacts of various management
alternatives on the subject allotments. Then, on August 21, 2019, the BLM published the
proposed EA along with the Proposed Decisions for all of the subject subregion
allotments. The field manager determined that wildfire-related conditions could be
improved over the course of the ten-year permits by increasing livestock grazing levels
in areas where non-native grasses crowded out native vegetation, thereby allowing
sagebrush communities to expand.
BLM received twelve protests of the Proposed Decisions from grazing
permittees, two protests from Wildlands Defense and Western Watersheds Project, and
one protest from the Idaho Cattle Association. In response, BLM amended the initial
EA, resulting in the Revised EA issued in February 2020. Revised EA, pp. 2-3; BER
042485-042486. The Final Decisions for seventeen of the 28 subject allotments were
issued on February 28, 2020. The Final Decisions for the remaining eleven allotments in
Group 2 were issued on June 15, 2020.

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
STANDARD OF REVIEW FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT
To obtain Summary Judgment there must be no material, substantive issue of
fact in dispute between the parties. Larson v. BLM, 129 IBLA 250, 252 (1994). Generally
speaking, the Departmental Cases Hearings Division, as well as the Interior Board of
Land Appeals (“IBLA”), in practice follow the rules of summary judgment set out
under Rule 56 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, under which all factual
inferences must be drawn in the light most favorable to the non-moving party, drawing
all reasonable inferences in its favor. Dannelle and Chad Hensley, et al., 195 IBLA 345,
354 (2020). Summary Judgment is authorized where the evidence establishes that there
is no genuine issue as to any material fact and where the moving party, therefore, is
entitled to a judgment as a matter of law. Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242,
247 (1986).
Once the moving party has met its burden, the burden then shifts to the non-
moving party to set forth by affidavit, or other means, specific facts showing that there
is a genuine issue of material fact or that, legally, the moving party is not entitled to
judgment. T.W. Electric Service, Inc. v. Pacific Electric Contractors Association, 809 F.2d
626, 630 (9th Cir. 1987). Legal memoranda are not evidence and do not create issues of
fact capable of defeating an otherwise valid motion for summary Judgment. British
Airways Board v. Boeing Company, 585 F.2d 946, 952 (9th Cir. 1987).
SUMMARY OF JRS’ CONTENTIONS
JRS contends that BLM’s alleged NEPA-related legal error is based upon the
following considerations:
BLM seeks to backfill its revised EA after-the-fact. BLM provides no
justification for this backfilling. It can be assumed that given the
additional time BLM took between the issuance of the Revised EA on
February 28, 2020, and the issuance of the Final Decisions
dated June 15, 2020, BLM found additional reasons to rationalize its
Revised EA as related to the Coonskin-EJD and Pigtail Butte Allotments.
However, this cannot lawfully occur since this supplementation on June
15, 2020, was not made in any new or
additional NEPA document.
JRS Motion, pp. 5-6.
13

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
Appellant generally contends that the June 15, 2020, Final Decisions covering the
Coonskin-EJD and Pigtail Butte Allotments provided different reasons, not set forth in
the February 28, 2020, Revised EA, in order to further rationalize and update the
Revised EA, without taking additional formal NEPA action to update or amend the
Revised EA. JRS Motion, p. 9; also see: Helmick Declaration, Paras. 10,11, 13 & Helmick
Exhibits 3 & 4. Helmick Exhibit 3 addresses further alleged reasons by BLM to
rationalize the February Revised EA with respect to the Cookskin-EJD Allotment, which
were not previously addressed in the Revised EA. Helmick Declaration, Paras. 10, 13.
Similarly, it is further contended by Appellant that Helmick Exhibit 4 discloses further
reasons set out by BLM in its June 15, 2020, Final Decision regarding the Pigtail Butte
Allotment that were not included in the February 2020 Revised EA. Helmick
Declaration, Paras. 10, 11, 13.
In arguing the legal merits of its contention that BLM violated NEPA by not
formally updating the Revised EA for purposes of issuing the June 2020 Group 2 Final
Decisions, Appellant relies in part upon Washington County, Utah, 185 IBLA 39, 50-51
(2014). Therein, the Board concluded that “Absent the necessary explanation and
supporting record for an agency decision, we have long held that it is appropriate to set
aside the decision and remand the case to BLM for compilation of a more complete
record and readjudication of the matter.” Ibid. Relatedly, JRS concludes the following:
Here, like Washington County, Utah, BLM provides different reasons, not
set forth in the Revised EA, to rationalize its Revised EA dated February
28, 2020, in later-issued Final Decisions dated June 15, 2020. Helmick
Declaration, Exhibits, 3, 4. These differences are revealed by reviewing
the new language, revised language, or edited language within Final
Decisions. See Helmick Declaration Paras. 10, 11, 13. The differences have
direct, consequence to JRS (particularly given Guerry and JRS are
authorized in the same allotments as common permittees).
JRS Motion, pp. 14-15; emphasis in original.
JRS then provides a detailed chart of the new, revised, or edited language which
appears in the June decisions, as distinguished from the February decisions covering
the same allotments. Each portion thereof also includes a summary of the consequences
of said differences. JRS Motion, pp. 15-23. For example, the Guerry Decision required
that “All troughs and open water storage tanks must have functional wildlife escape
ramps. It is the permittee’s responsibility to install all escape ramps.” However, the
JRS Decision required “all troughs and open water storage tanks must have a BLM-
provided wildlife escape ramp. It is the permittee’s responsibility to install and
14

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
maintain all escape ramps consistent with current BLM policy.” The consequence,
according to JRS is that “The Revised EA provided no rationale for why Guerry must
only provide ‘functional … ramps’, while JRS has to provide ‘BLM-provided … ramps.’
This is a more restrictive standard as to JRS which will delay maintenance to wildlife
escape ramps. Helmick Declaration, Exhibit 3, Number 5; Helmick Declaration, Exhibit
4, Number 4.” JRS Motion, p.16. Throughout the referenced chart, it is JRS’ contention
that more restrictive standards were imposed upon JRS than upon Guerry, and that
these more restrictive requirements were not legally rationalized in the February 2020
Revised EA, consequently allegedly requiring an updated and amended EA prior to the
issuance of the June 2020 Final Decisions.
CONTENTIONS OF BLM
With respect to the allotments whose Final Decisions were postponed until June
2020, BLM, on the other hand, has argued the following:
Due to the length and breadth of protests from permittees associated with
the remaining 11 allotments, BLM needed an additional three months to
respond to them. See Exhibit 1, Declaration of Elliot Traher, included as
an attachment to this motion, Paras. 7-9. The final decisions and
responses to protests for the 11 allotments were issued on June 15, 2020.
While the responses to protests were detailed, the decisions themselves
followed the management outlined in the February 28, 2020 decisions
for other allotments in the subregion, which in turn closely resembled
the management described in the August 2019 decisions.
BLM’s Motion, p. 4; Emphasis added.
After BLM’s issuance of its earlier Proposed Decisions, both Guerry and JRS filed
protests of the Proposed Decisions, after which the authorized officer reconsidered
those decisions and revised the EA to analyze those issues raised in the protests that
legally required additional environmental analyses. This was followed by the issuance
of Final Decisions and the Revised EA in February 2020. And, it was because of the
voluminous content of the JRS protests that the Group 2 dockets were delayed for Final
Decisions until June 2020.
JRS further contends that, unlike Guerry, it is uniquely required to obtain BLM’s
written permission before it may construct, maintain, or modify range improvements,
that it must use BLM’s wildlife escape ramps, and that it must consult with more than
the BLM wildlife biologist in designated circumstances. This contention is misplaced,
15

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
because BLM must provide written approval before construction, repair, modification,
or replacement of any and all range improvements. 43 C.F.R. 4120.3-1. This regulation
applies equally to both Guerry and JRS.
With respect to the Final Decisions and BLM’s responses to protests covering the
eleven allotments that were the subjects of the June 15, 2020, Final Decisions, BLM’s
responses to the protests were appropriately detailed; however, the eleven decisions
themselves reiterated the management terms and conditions that were included in the
February 28, 2020, Final Decisions that covered the other subject allotments in the
subregion. As stated by government counsel, with respect to management of the
allotments, all of the Final Decisions for the subject subregion, “… closely resembled the
management described in the August 2019 proposed decisions.” BLM’s Motion. P. 4.
BLM extends its argument in its Response Brief, as follows:
JRS properties true challenge is whether BLM must justify every minute
difference between grazing decisions that pertain to allotments JRS
Properties shares with Guerry, Inc. JRS Properties’ brief focuses on minor
differences between the BLM’s final grazing decisions addressing
livestock use of the Coonskin-EJD and Pigtail Butte allotments …. JRS
Properties’ arguments provide no basis for reversal or remand because (1)
BLM’s grazing decisions are supported by the record as a whole,
including the EA; (2) BLM need not justify differences between grazing
decisions ….
BLM’s Response, p. 1.
Relatedly, none of the differences between the Guerry, Inc. and JRS Properties
Final Decisions materially alter BLM’s objectives or management of the two subject
allotments. For example, JRS contends that it is subject to more restrictive monitoring
standards with respect to incremental increases in livestock. However, both of the
decisions require that BLM may not approve an increase in AUMs if monitoring data
shows that limits in the Management Guidelines are likely to be exceeded. Guerry Final
Decision, p. 13, BER 043210; JRS Properties Final Decision, p. 14, BER2 078864.
JRS argues that it is subject to greater monitoring than Guerry, because its
Coonskin-EJD decision states that BLM will monitor in accordance with agency
priorities and resource limitations; whereas, Guerry, Inc.’s decision states that
monitoring will be based on agency priorities alone. JRS Properties’ Final Decision, p.
17, BER2 078867; Guerry, Inc. Final Decision, pp. 16-17,BER 043213-043214. The Revised
16

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
EA states that monitoring frequency will be based on both management priorities and
resource concerns. Revised EA, p. 15, BER 042499. The monitoring standard, therefore,
applies equally to JRS and Guerry.
In its Response Brief, BLM further states that, “BLM’s decision mistakenly based
its increases on average actual use rather than permitted use. While that error resulted
in a minor difference for the Coonskin-EJD allotment (10,259 AUMS rather than 10,257
AUMs for JRS Properties), the difference for the Pigtail Butte allotment is much greater:
3,910 AUMs for JRS Properties rather than the 3,330 allocated in the final grazing
decision. BLM requests that the ALJ correct the errors in its final orders by allocating:
Guerry, Inc.: Pigtail Butte, 2,479 AUMs, Coonskin-EJD, 3,257 AUMs. JRS Properties:
Pigtail Butte, 3,910 AUMs, Coonskin-EJD, 10,259 AUMs.” BLM’s Response Brief, p. 9.
Because JRS’ Motion For Summary Judgment, as well as, JRS’ ensuing Response
and Reply Briefs do not in any context address the issue of “mistaken” AUMs, it is my
determination to reserve any ruling on this issue with respect to the above-referenced
JRS dockets, because JRS’ Motion does not address the “mistaken” AUMs issue.
DISCUSSION
The Interior Board Of Land Appeals (“IBLA”), has determined the relevant
standard for review of an EA, as follows:
When BLM concludes in a FONSI that it is not necessary to prepare an EIS
and proceeds on the basis of an EA, its decision will be deemed to comply
with NEPA where the record demonstrates that BLM considered all
relevant matters of environmental concern, took a ‘hard look’ at potential
environmental impacts, and made a convincing case that no significant
impact will result or that any such impact will be reduced to
insignificance by the adoption of appropriate mitigation measures. …
In assessing the adequacy of an EA, we are guided by the ‘rule of reason’
and recognize that, in an EA, BLM need only briefly discuss the likely
impacts of the proposed action: ‘By nature, it is intended to be an
overview of environmental concerns, not an exhaustive study of all
environmental issues which the project raises.’ Since the purpose of an
EA is to assess whether the potential impacts of the proposed action
are likely to be significant, it may be a ‘concise public document’ that
‘briefly’ discusses ‘the environmental impacts of the proposed action and
alternatives.’ Thus, an EA will not be set aside ‘merely because the EA
17

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
could have been more thorough,’ because the burden is on the appellant
to show that any omitted analysis ‘compromised the EA so severely as to
render the FONSI arbitrary and capricious.’
Bureau of Land Management v. Western Watersheds Project & Wild Utah Project, 191
IBLA 144, 149-151 (2017).
Therefore, the fundamental issue becomes the following: Was the content of the
Revised EA issued in February 2020, within the four corners thereof, legally sufficient
on its face to justify the accompanying FONSI and to adequately analyze relevant
environmental issues covering all of the Group 1 and Group 2 subregion Final
Decisions? In my opinion, the answer to that question is yes, because if one completely
deletes or ignores BLM’s referenced responses to the various public comments, which
responses were included in the eleven June 2020 Final Decisions, the Revised EA
remains legally sufficient on its face, within the four corners of the Revised EA, to
support and justify the FONSI, as well as, each of the eleven June 2020 Final Decisions.
IBLA has addressed a similar issue, under analogous factual circumstances, as
follows:
In the present case, there is no issue regarding the public disclosure for
comment of data compiled regarding the impacts of the Lisbon Valley
Project leading up to and including the issuance of the FEIS and ROD.
Following issuance of the FEIS and ROD, Appellants filed their appeal,
and thereafter, new information was generated. It is this new information
that Appellants argue must be distributed for public comment
or NEPA requirements will be violated.
We disagree. The new information does not radically change an
assumption of the FEIS, or relate directly to an alternative action, or show
that there are significant impacts of the project that were not disclosed in
the FEIS. In fact, the new information confirmed the assumption of the
FEIS that the Navajo Aquifer was a Class III aquifer, and it also arguably
establishes that impacts to ground water quality will be minimal. In
addition, BLM sent copies of all the new information to Appellants and
the information was publicly available. The groundwater data and
analyses were also submitted to the State of Utah, which classified the
18

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
Navajo Aquifer as Class III. The fact that the information was not released
expressly for public comment is not, under the facts of this case, a
violation of NEPA.
National Wildlife Federation, ET AL., 145 IBLA 348, 365 (1998); emphasis added.
BLM’s Revised EA was intended to cover all of the subregion subject allotments
in both Group 1 and Group 2. BLM’s Final Decisions covering all of the allotments
were divided into two groups, Group 1 and Group 2, because of the large number of
public comments that were submitted with respect to the eleven decisions that
ultimately were included in the June 2020 Group 2. Had it not been for the large
number of public comments that were received by BLM covering the allotments in
Group 2, it is apparent that BLM would have issued all of the Final Decisions in
February 2020.
In plain terms, JRS contends that BLM’s Group 2 responses to the Group 2
permittees’ public comments regarding the Proposed Decisions, constituted additional
rationalizations that should have been included in the February 2020 Revised EA or
been addressed in a further revised, updated EA covering the Group 2 June 2020 Final
Decisions. This argument would be correct, if and only if, the February 2020 Revised
EA was, within its four corners, legally insufficient in content to environmentally
support the FONSI, as well as, both the Group 1 February 2020 Final Decisions and the
Group 2 June 2020 Final Decisions. However, it is my determination that the February
2020 Revised EA remains legally sufficient on its face, given its content, to adequately
support both the FONSI and all of the Group 1 and Group 2 Final Decisions, just as
would have been the case had no public comments been submitted by the permittees
and responded to by BLM. In particular, the Revised EA analyzes a legally sufficient
number of alternatives; the Revised EA takes the requisite “hard look” at relevant
environmental issues and impacts; and, the Revised EA includes legally sufficient
analyses of relevant cumulative impacts, covering all of the allotments in Group 1 and
Group 2. Given this, the fact that BLM went on to fully address the Group 2 public
comments did not serve to automatically negate the legal sufficiency of the Revised EA
to cover all of the Group 1 and Group 2 Final Decisions.
19

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
CONCLUSION
For the above-stated reasons, it is my determination that BLM’s February 2020
Revised EA was legally sufficient to support the associated FONSI, as well as all of the
Group 1 and Group 2 Final Decisions. Consequently, Appellant JRS’s Motion For
Summary Judgment is hereby DENIED; BLM’s Motion For Summary Judgment is
GRANTED.
